loro-piana.types: Loro Piana is a maison and cloth brand, not a cashmere grade by itself. Separate generic fibers (cashmere, wool, silk), mill collections (including names that appear in other brands’ educational stories, such as Pecora Nera), and producer finishes (Storm System on documented cloths). Cashmere micron bands and wool Super S cloth numbers answer different questions than a maison logo.
loro-piana.fabrics: Public association includes soft cashmere knits and woven coatings, fine wool suiting and outerwear cloths, and weather-finished fabrics where the producer names Storm System. Treat each SKU’s ticket as authoritative. Open tropical wool weaves and dense winter cloths show how structure, not logo, drives seasonality.
loro-piana.quality: Ask for fiber percentages, any stated mean diameter or cashmere grade language, cloth weight and whether a weather finish is actually specified. Producer finish pages describe intended water and wind behavior; they are not universal properties of every maison product. Prefer measurable tickets over adjectives such as precious or iconic.
pros: Maison pages can illustrate how mill finishing brands sit above generic fiber names.
Storm System documentation (producer) teaches finish-versus-fiber literacy when cited carefully.
Cashmere and fine-wool examples clarify noble-fiber vocabulary.
cons: Luxury branding can obscure farm geography and labor detail.
Finish trademarks are easy to over-generalize across the whole label.
Collection names are not fiber classes.
loro-piana.impact: Cashmere and wool impacts concentrate in grazing systems, processing water and chemistry, and garment care longevity. Maison marketing may reference traceability programs; verify the program name and scope on the product. A weather finish can extend wear life for some users but adds chemistry that should be disclosed in care.
loro-piana.care: Follow the care label on each SKU. Cashmere knits usually need gentle washing or professional care and must dry flat to keep shape. Weather-finished cloths may require wipe-clean or reproof steps described by the producer for that finish. Avoid high heat that can damage keratin fibers and polymer finish films alike; air garments between wears.
faq: Is Loro Piana a fiber?
No. Loro Piana is a textile maison trademark. Cashmere or wool written on the label is the fiber class; the maison name is commerce, design and finishing.
What is Storm System?
Storm System is a Loro Piana producer finish name for weather-resistant behavior on documented cloths. It is not a fiber and applies only where the producer specifies it for that product.
Is Pecora Nera a fiber class?
No. Pecora Nera is a mill collection name that appears in cloth stories. Always read the generic fiber content line for the legal composition of the cloth or garment.
Does this atlas link Loro Piana on the map?
No. Reference maison entries do not receive invented mill-brand map edges. Use producer pages for any supply claims rather than the atlas globe.
notable: Base material link in this atlas: cashmere, with wool cloths discussed in prose.
Storm System cited only as producer-attributed finish language.
Biella marks maison or processing geography, not automatic farm origin.

piacenza-1733.types: Piacenza 1733 is a mill-house identity, not a micron grade. Keep distinct: generic wool (and other noble fibers the mill may publish), cloth constructions for apparel and interiors, and the house trademark with its Pollone / Biella place story. Founding-year marketing is heritage narrative, not a lab measurement.
piacenza-1733.fabrics: Producer channels emphasize wool fabrics and knitwear alongside seasonal cloth collections for apparel. Use them as examples of mill-house output from the Biella district rather than as a single historic handfeel. Compare weight, weave, yarn count and finish across cloths when studying modern products from a long-lived mill.
piacenza-1733.quality: Look for fiber content, cloth weight, yarn quality and finishing notes on tickets and hangtags. A 1733 founding claim on producer story pages is heritage narrative, not a laboratory quality metric. Prefer even yarn, clean selvedges, secure seams and documented care instructions over antiquity adjectives alone.
pros: Historic mill-house stories teach place-based textile literacy.
Biella clustering illustrates why mill names differ from farm origin.
Producer story pages give attributed heritage dates to cite carefully.
cons: Heritage marketing can outrun SKU-level transparency.
Long history does not equal verified farm practice.
English and Italian producer pages may differ in detail.
No atlas map edges from heritage claims.
piacenza-1733.impact: Wool mill impacts include water and energy in scouring and finishing and chemical management in dyehouses. Family-mill sustainability claims should be read on current producer pages with dates and clear scope. Longevity of garments and repair culture often matter as much as the mill’s founding century when judging practical footprint.
piacenza-1733.care: Defer to the product care label for washing, drying and ironing limits. Wool cloths often prefer airing, gentle brushing and professional pressing rather than frequent machine washing. Knitwear from wool mills usually needs a gentle cycle or hand wash and flat drying; store pieces clean to discourage keratin pests.
faq: Is Piacenza 1733 a fiber?
No. It is a historic Biella mill-house trademark. Wool or other fibers named on the label remain the generic materials, separate from the house identity.
Does 1733 mean the wool is Italian-grown?
No. The year is a producer founding story for the mill house. Fiber origin is a separate question from where cloth was spun, woven or finished.
Where does the producer place the mill?
Public producer pages locate Fratelli Piacenza / Piacenza 1733 in Pollone in the Biella textile district of Piedmont, Italy, as the house geography.
Will the atlas draw a route to Piacenza?
No. Reference mill-house brands do not receive invented map edges. Heritage narratives stay in prose and citations, not in globe logistics.
notable: Educational role: mill-house provenance versus fiber class.
No proprietary fiber implied by the house name.

paul-smith.types: Paul Smith is not a wool grade. Track three layers when you read a hangtag: the generic fiber such as wool, cotton, linen or a blend; the cloth construction and finish; and the designer house trademark that names the collection rather than the keratin. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
paul-smith.fabrics: Educational examples include tailored jackets and trousers in wool or wool-rich cloths and cotton shirts with mill or seasonal cloth names. Always read the SKU composition because the house trademark spans many fabric stories across seasons. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
paul-smith.quality: Prefer clear fiber percentages, cloth weight or season cues, and honest blend disclosure over designer adjectives alone. A famous house name cannot replace micron data, weave description or a complete care label when you are studying materials. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
pros: Designer storytelling can name cloth and make details learners can unpack.
Useful foil when teaching that a fashion house is not a fiber.
Hangtags often still carry generic fiber names required by labeling law.
cons: A designer trademark does not standardize cloth across seasons.
House branding can be mistaken for farm origin or mill ownership.
Wide product range means there is no single fiber profile for the brand.
paul-smith.impact: Impact follows fiber farming, dyeing and finishing, garment transport and wear life for each product. This atlas does not assign a single house-level footprint, because Paul Smith garments are not one fiber system. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
paul-smith.care: Follow the garment care label without exception. Wool suiting often needs pressing and rest between wears, while cotton shirts follow ordinary wash or dry-clean instructions printed on the care panel. This atlas treats the trademark as educational vocabulary for reading hangtags, mill cloth names and generic fiber classes without certifying supply chains, performance claims or animal welfare.
faq: Is Paul Smith a type of wool?
No. Paul Smith is a designer house trademark. The fiber remains wool or whatever the legal composition panel states for that garment.
Why is it in Fibers of Earth?
As a reference brand for practicing materials language in designer menswear, separating house, mill cloth and generic fiber on the ticket.
Does the house make its own fiber?
No proprietary fiber chemistry is implied. Cloth and fiber are specified or sourced per product through ordinary textile supply chains.
